name: Aramaic, Middle Aramaic period 200 BC-AD 200
catalog_citation: Creason, Stuart. 2004. 'Aramaic'. In Roger D. Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages, ch. 13, pp. 391-426. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
catalog_locator: ch. 13 'Aramaic' (Stuart Creason), sec. 3.5 'Stress', p. 400 (page confirmed: the scanned header '400 / The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages…
catalog_quote: 3.5 Stress There is one primary stressed syllable in each Aramaic word (with the exception of some particles; see 884.6, 4.7.4, and 4.8.1). In Proto-Aramaic, words having a final closed syllable were stressed on that syllable; and words having a final open syllable were stressed on the penultimate syllable, regardless of the length of the word-final vowel. At a very early stage, word-final short vowels were either lost or lengthened and so the stressed, open penultimate syllable of words with a final short vowel became the final stressed, closed syllable. Stress remained on this syllable and the rules regarding stress were not altered. These rules remain unaltered throughout most of the history of Aramaic, though in some dialects of Late Aramaic, stress shifted from the final syllable to the penultimate syllable in some or all words which had a closed final syllable.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Locator check: the excerpt file reproduces lines 33715-33722 and 34273-34286 of the on-disk archive.org scanned; I re-read those the scanned textdirectly (sed 34255-34300) and the sec. 3.5 'Stress' paragraph is there word for word. The report's quote is verbatim apart from two marked ellipses (the omitted text is 'see §§4.6, 4.7.4, and 4.8.1' [scanned '884.6'] and the closing 'syllable in some or all words which had a closed final syllable'). Authorship/identity of the source confirmed: the scanned text 'CHAPTER 13 / Aramaic / STUART CREASON'; sec. 1.2.3 (lines 33715ff) defines 'Middle Aramaic (200 BC-AD 200)' as 'most notably Palmyrene, Hatran, Nabatean, and the dialect of the Aramaic text…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One main stress per word, at the right edge: a word ending in a closed syllable is stressed on that final syllable; a word ending in an open syllable is stressed on the penult. Since final short vowels were lost early, most words end in a stressed closed final syllable, so surface stress is predominantly final; the author holds this system constant from Old through Middle Aramaic (Qumran, Nabataean, Palmyrene, Hatran), with retraction to the penult only in some Late Aramaic dialects.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (only 'one primary stressed syllable in each Aramaic word').
new_statements.exceptions: Some particles carry no stress of their own (proclitic prepositions/particles, cross-referenced to his §§4.6, 4.7.4, 4.8.1); penultimate shift in 'some dialects of Late Aramaic' (outside this node). Note dissent: Beyer (1986: 25, 39, deferring to ATTM 1984: 142-146) treats general final stress as arising only after the 7th c. AD and for 1st-c. Judaean/Galilean states only that suffix -ī 'my' bore the stress while other unstressed long final vowels were lost.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated diachronically for Aramaic as a whole (Proto-Aramaic through Late Aramaic); for the Middle Aramaic corpora (unvocalised consonantal script) it is a reconstruction, not read off pointed texts or recordings. Segert 1975 §3.5 gives the same predominantly-final picture but explicitly on the authority of the Tiberian Masoretic tradition of Biblical Aramaic.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's midd1366 is Fitzmyer's 'Middle Aramaic' stage node (dialects: Dead Sea-New Testament Aramaic dead1234, Nabatean naba1259, Palmyrene palm1242, Hatran hatr1234), all known only from unvocalised consonantal texts. The quoted source (Creason 2004) is a pan-Aramaic handbook sketch that explicitly includes this period (Palmyrene, Hatran, Nabatean, Qumran) in its scope but states the stress rule diachronically for Aramaic as a whole, not per variety; no variety-specific description opened (Cantineau 1930 Nabataean, Rosenthal 1936 Palmyrene, Muraoka 2011 Qumran [TOC], Machiela 2022 Qumran, Marcato 2018 Hatran) states where stress falls. Beyer 1986 (pp.25, 39-40; -> ATTM 142-146) holds a dissenting chronology (general final stress only post-7th c. AD) and gives only morpheme-level stress facts for 1st-c. Judaean/Galilean. The earlier scan's pointer to Nöldeke's Syriac grammar concerns Classical Syriac (clas1252), a different Glottolog language.
